summary.text: 出 depicts a foot stepping out of an enclosure. Early inscriptions use it for going out and sending out, though they do not show when those related uses developed.

formation.text: Early forms are analyzed as the pictorial combination of a foot, 止, and an enclosure, 凵; some oracle-bone forms use 囗 for the enclosure. An older lexicographic account instead describes plants growing upward, a reading associated with the later, less recognizable form.

components.text: In early forms, 止 depicts the foot moving outward. Later forms made this element less recognizable.
凵 depicts the enclosure or hollow from which the foot moves. Some oracle-bone forms use 囗 in its place.

history.text: Early oracle-bone and bronze forms are analyzed as 止 above 凵; some oracle-bone forms use 囗. The curated oracle-script image is a modern redraw, not an artifact photograph, and does not identify a dated specimen.
A graphic analysis proposes that the parts later joined and 止 came to resemble 屮 in later scripts. This may explain the plant-growth interpretation, but the precise sequence is not established.

uncertainties.text: The cited inscriptions do not establish a securely dated first use or the relative chronology of all the character’s meanings.
Different Old Chinese reconstructions are recorded for the spoken word or words written 出. They concern pronunciation, not a sound component in the graph.

evidence.text: A sprout 屮 growing out of a container 凵
Pictograph of a foot (止) going out of an enclosure.
進也。象艸木益滋，上出達也。凡出之屬皆从出。

Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 止 (“foot”) + 凵 (“cave”) – to step out of a cave; to exit. Compare 各.
By the Qin dynasty, the character has lost its original shape. Based on the distorted form, Shuowen mistakenly interprets the character as a pictogram of a plant (屮) growing outwards.
STEDT derives this word as a cognate of Proto-Tibeto-Burman *s-twak (“to come or go out; to emerge”); compare Burmese ထွက် (htwak, “to go or come out; to produce or yield; to leave”), Proto-Lolo-Burmese *ʔ-twakᴴ (“to come or got out; to emerge”), Proto-Kuki-Chin *tshuak-I, *tshuaʔ-II (“to come out; to emerge; to appear”). But virtually all Old Chinese reconstructions of this word nowadays are completely phonetically incompatible with this etymon; this comparison should be rejected.
Alternatively, Sagart (1999) and Baxter and Sagart (2014) suggest that this word is related to other words that express extraction, such as 掘 (OC *[ɡ]ut, “to dig out”), and reconstruct the Old Chinese with an intransitivizing prefix *t-.
進也。象艸木益滋，上出達也。凡出之屬皆从出。

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解；甲骨文、金文、簡帛形體；《說文》及廣韻條目
evidence.text: The database analyzes 出 in oracle-bone and bronze forms as 止 (a foot) over 凵, with some oracle-bone forms using 囗. It interprets 凵/囗 as a cave or dwelling and the graph as a foot stepping outside, with the original sense ‘go out’. It cites oracle-bone examples 合集5063 王出 (‘the king goes out’), 合集33006 出日 (‘sunrise’), and 合集7205 勿出兵 (‘do not send out troops’); the first is an attested motion use, while the latter examples show contextual extensions. It also cites bronze inscriptions for going out, paying/issuing cloth, issuing commands, and transmitting commands. These examples support early use in multiple related contexts but do not by themselves establish the chronology of each sense. The entry records two Guangyun fanqie readings, 尺類 and 赤律, in departing and entering tone categories respectively. The source reproduces Shuowen’s ‘進也。象艸木益滋上出達也’, which is an early lexicographic account, not independent confirmation of the graph’s earliest form.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「出」

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, 漢字字形演變資料庫
evidence.text: The database describes the upper part in oracle-bone and bronze forms as 止, representing a foot, and the lower part as a cave-like shape: together, a person stepping outward. This supports the foot-and-enclosure interpretation independently of the Shuowen plant explanation. The page lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript and small-seal categories; its bronze examples include inscription 集成05410. The accessible text does not date individual oracle-bone specimens or spell out a full dated sequence of graphic changes.
evidence.title: 漢字「出」：字形演變

evidence.text: This page describes oracle-bone and bronze 出 as 止 plus 凵, and reports an oracle-bone variant with 囗 instead of 凵, understood as an enclosure/dwelling. It proposes that the feet and enclosure later joined graphically, making the seal form less transparent; in clerical and regular scripts the 止 component became distorted toward a form read as 屮. The page indexes examples from oracle-bone inscriptions (including 合集217 and 合集33050), bronze inscriptions including Western Zhou vessels, Warring States texts, the Shuowen seal form, and the Qin Shuihudi manuscript 睡.效60. Its period labels establish source contexts but no exact first-use date; its account is a source’s analysis, not a direct visual inspection in this research.
evidence.title: 汉字「出」字形演变字源

evidence.source: Baley, “Reconstructing Old Chinese *-ts Using Han-Time Material,” Transactions of the Philological Society
evidence.text: The article reports Baxter and Sagart’s Old Chinese reconstructions for the two uses written 出: Middle Chinese tsyhwit ‘go or come out’ corresponds to OC *t-kʰut, and Middle Chinese tsyhwijH ‘bring or take out’ to OC *t-kʰut-s. It explains that the departing-tone reading’s proposed *-ut-s is supported by its graphic/lexical connection with the entering-tone reading in *-ut. This is a phonological and word-family analysis, not evidence for an extra graphic component or a whole-graph loan. The article presents these reconstructions as Baxter–Sagart’s analysis; it does not independently establish every semantic derivation between the two verbs.
evidence.title: Reconstructing Old Chinese *‐ts Using Han‐Time Material

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.

search_audit.query: site:ctext.org/shuo-wen-jie-zi/chu-bu 出 說文; 出 甲骨文 合集5063 王出; 勿出兵 合集7205
search_audit.outcome: The Ctext page returned 403 and could not be inspected. The CUHK entry was inspected and supplies the cited oracle-bone examples; no precise date for the individual inscriptions was established.

gaps: The accessed sources do not supply a securely dated earliest oracle-bone token; they identify inscription numbers and broad material categories. The first attested graph and the dating of its earliest use therefore remain unestablished here.

The dossier’s sprout-from-container account is traceable to Shuowen’s own explanation, but the inspected paleographic sources instead analyze early forms as foot plus enclosure. The proposed Qin-era distortion explains the later plant reading, but the specific transition is supported here by a secondary collation rather than a primary glyph-by-glyph study.

The entry cites early oracle-bone and bronze contexts for ‘go out’, sunrise, sending troops, paying cloth, and issuing/transmitting commands, but these selected examples do not establish a complete semantic chronology or the precise links among extensions such as ‘produce’, ‘stand’, and ‘send out’.

No sound component is proposed in the paleographic analysis, so component-specific sound comparison is inapplicable. Baxter–Sagart reconstructions concern the spoken verb(s) recorded by 出, not a phonetic subcomponent.

The repository includes Zhengzhang reconstructions (*kʰljuds / *kʰljud) that differ from Baxter–Sagart *t-kʰut / *t-kʰut-s. No primary Zhengzhang source was inspected to assess the rationale or dialect/variant scope of that comparison.

A search result mentions a Proto-Tibeto-Burman comparison, but no source directly establishing its proposed cognacy or sound history was inspected. The dossier’s caution that most Old Chinese reconstructions are phonetically incompatible is not independently verified here.

The Chinese CUHK entry provides cited readings and Guangyun fanqie, but this research did not verify a modern pronunciation reference for Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, Korean, or Vietnamese; the dossier’s modern readings remain repository metadata.
The Zdic attempt failed with a fetch timeout. No glyph images were visually inspected.

The inspected sources identify oracle-bone examples, including 合集5063 王出, but do not provide a securely dated earliest token or a precise date for that inscription. The earliest attested graph and an exact first-use date remain unestablished here.

The early foot-plus-enclosure analysis is supported by paleographic database descriptions. The proposed sequence in which the parts joined and 止 later became visually confused with 屮 is stated by a secondary collation; a primary glyph-by-glyph demonstration of that transition was not inspected.

The oracle-bone examples include motion, sunrise, and sending troops; bronze examples include going out, paying cloth, and issuing or transmitting commands. These examples do not establish a complete chronological sequence or the semantic links to later senses such as ‘produce’ and ‘stand’.

No phonetic component is proposed by the inspected paleographic analyses. The readings and Old Chinese reconstructions concern the spoken word(s) written 出, not an internal sound component. The dossier’s Zhengzhang reconstructions differ from Baxter–Sagart’s; their rationale and variant scope were not independently checked against a primary Zhengzhang source.

No independent evidence was found here for the proposed Tibeto-Burman cognacy, or for a historical whole-graph borrowing involving 出. The modern and later dictionary glosses do not by themselves establish either claim.

The Zdic page lists several meanings and citations, but this research did not verify the dates of all cited texts or establish chronology from that gloss list. The specific histories of ‘send out’, ‘produce’, ‘stand’, and the ‘scene/section’ use associated with 齣 remain unresolved.

No glyph image was visually inspected. The one proposed file is described by its source page as a modern vector redraw, not an ancient artifact photograph. Its direct file fetch failed with a cache miss.

items.period: Shang-period oracle-bone script tradition; the file description does not date an individual specimen
items.tradition: Oracle-bone script; modern digital vector redraw
items.caption: An oracle-bone-script form of 出, shown here as a modern vector redraw. Paleographic analyses read the upper shape as a foot and the lower shape as an enclosure, suggesting a figure stepping out.
items.alt: Black oracle-bone-style glyph on a light background, with an irregular upper form joined to a broad curved lower enclosure; modern vector redraw.
items.selection_reason: This candidate visibly illustrates the foot-and-enclosure interpretation supported for early forms of 出.
items.rights: Public domain, as marked in the file description; verify the file-page statement when reusing.

limitations.text: This is a modern redraw attributed to oracle-bone script, not an artifact photograph. Its individual specimen and exact date are not established, and the cited sources do not identify the earliest attested form.
